content.body: Imagine you have a social network diagram showing friends connected to friends. How would you make an exact copy of that entire network? Today we'll learn how to clone a graph—creating a perfect duplicate while exploring connections without getting stuck in loops.
content.title: What we'll learn

content.body:
By the end of this lesson, you'll be able to:
1. Explain why we need to track visited nodes when copying graphs
2. Implement a graph cloning algorithm using depth-first search
3. Avoid infinite loops when graphs contain cycles
4. Create new nodes while preserving neighbor relationships
content.title: Learning goals

content.body: Look at this simple graph with 3 nodes: A connects to B, B connects to C. If you start at A and want to copy everything, where would you go first? What's the natural path your eyes follow when exploring these connections?
content.title: Explore the network

content.body: Now add a connection from C back to A, creating a triangle: A→B→C→A. If you start copying at A, then go to B, then to C... where does C point you back to? What happens if you keep following connections without a plan?
content.title: Add a cycle
content.visualMetaphor: A ↔ B ↔ C (triangle with bidirectional arrows showing cycles)

content.body: You probably followed connections naturally—A to B to C. But with the cycle, you might have felt you were going in circles. That's exactly what happens in code: without tracking, we'd revisit nodes forever.
content.title: What you noticed

content.body: Real graphs can have hundreds of nodes with complex connections. If we don't track where we've been, we'll waste time copying the same node multiple times or get stuck in infinite loops. We need a way to explore efficiently.
content.title: Why tracking matters

content.body: The core concept for graph problems is marking nodes as 'visited' as soon as we encounter them. This prevents revisiting and ensures we explore each connection exactly once. Think of it like leaving breadcrumbs—once you've copied a node, you don't need to copy it again.
content.title: Key idea: visited tracking
content.visualMetaphor: Show visited (colored) vs unvisited (gray) nodes; paths that don't circle back to visited nodes

content.body: We'll use depth-first search with a visited map: 1) Start at the given node, 2) Create a copy, 3) Mark original as visited (store original→copy mapping), 4) Recursively copy all neighbors, 5) Connect copies just like originals. The map prevents infinite loops and duplicate copies.
content.title: The approach

content.body:
1. Create a map to track visited nodes (original → copy)
2. Define a recursive copy function
3. If node is already in map, return its copy (base case)
4. Otherwise, create new node with same value
5. Store mapping in visited map
6. For each neighbor: recursively copy it
7. Add copied neighbors to new node's list
8. Return the new node
content.title: Step-by-step logic

steps.title: Set up the visited map
steps.instruction: Create a Map to track which nodes we've already copied. This will prevent infinite loops when graphs have cycles.
steps.hint: Use 'new Map()' to create an empty map.
steps.feedbackCorrect: Perfect! The visited map will store original nodes as keys and their copies as values.
steps.feedbackPartial: You're on the right track. Remember to declare the map variable.
steps.feedbackWrong: Try creating a Map using 'new Map()'.

steps.title: Define the copy helper
steps.instruction: Create a recursive helper function 'dfs' that takes a node and returns its copy. This will do the actual copying work.
steps.hint: Define an inner function 'dfs' that accepts a node parameter.
steps.feedbackCorrect: Great! The dfs function will handle the recursive copying.
steps.feedbackPartial: Almost there. Make sure you define a function that takes a node parameter.
steps.feedbackWrong: Try defining a function like 'function dfs(originalNode) { }' inside cloneGraph.

steps.title: Base case: already visited
steps.instruction: Inside dfs, check if the node is already in the visited map. If yes, return the existing copy immediately.
steps.hint: Use visited.has() to check, then visited.get() to retrieve.
steps.feedbackCorrect: Excellent! This prevents infinite recursion and duplicate copies.
steps.feedbackPartial: Good start. Remember to return the copy if the node exists in visited.

steps.title: Create and store the copy
steps.instruction: If the node isn't visited, create a new Node with the same value. Store it in the visited map before copying neighbors.
steps.hint: Create new Node(originalNode.val), then visited.set(originalNode, copy).
steps.feedbackCorrect: Perfect! Storing immediately prevents infinite loops when neighbors reference back.
steps.feedbackPartial: Almost. Remember to both create the copy and store it in the map.
steps.feedbackWrong: Try: const copy = new Node(originalNode.val); visited.set(originalNode, copy);

steps.title: Copy all neighbors
steps.instruction: For each neighbor in originalNode.neighbors, recursively call dfs to get its copy, then add that copy to the current node's neighbors list.
steps.hint: Use a for...of loop over originalNode.neighbors, push dfs(neighbor) to copy.neighbors.
steps.feedbackCorrect: Well done! This recursively builds the entire graph structure.
steps.feedbackPartial: Good progress. Don't forget to actually add the copied neighbors to copy.neighbors.
steps.feedbackWrong: Try: for (let neighbor of originalNode.neighbors) { copy.neighbors.push(dfs(neighbor)); }

steps.title: Return and start the copy
steps.instruction: Return the copy from dfs, and at the end of cloneGraph, call dfs(node) to start the copying process (handling null case).
steps.hint: Add 'return copy;' at the end of dfs, and 'return node ? dfs(node) : null;' at the end of cloneGraph.
steps.feedbackCorrect: Excellent! You've implemented a complete graph cloning algorithm.
steps.feedbackPartial: Almost complete. Remember to return from both dfs and cloneGraph.
steps.feedbackWrong: Add 'return copy;' inside dfs, and 'return node ? dfs(node) : null;' at the end.

content.body: Congratulations! You've learned how to clone a graph using depth-first search with visited tracking. Remember: 1) Always mark nodes as visited immediately to prevent cycles, 2) The visited map serves both as tracking and original→copy lookup, 3) Recursively copy neighbors to preserve the graph structure. This pattern applies to many graph traversal problems.
